name: Eastern Newari
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Genetti, Carol 2007. A Grammar of Dolakha Newar. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter (full grammar with phonology chapter; paywalled). Also Genetti 1994 descriptive account.

new_statements.quote: [p.64] In Dolakha Newar, when words are pronounced in isolation, the first syllable is the most prominent, so can be said to be stressed. The primary cue for stress is pitch ... Length does not seem to be relevant to stress ... [p.68] It is possible to analyze the prominence on the initial syllable as resulting from an intonation pattern specific to words in isolation. At this point, there does not appear to be strong support of either analysis. What is clear is that if one analyzes Dolakha Newar as having first-syllable stress, it clearly has a very low functional load. It is predictable, not phonemic, and is largely obscured by intonation.
new_statements.citation: Genetti, Carol. 2007. A Grammar of Dolakha Newar (Mouton Grammar Library 40). Berlin/New York: Mouton de Gruyter.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 2 'Segmental phonetics and phonology', section 5 'Stress', p. 64 (opening) and p. 68 (conclusion); cf. p. 44 sec. 2.5.3
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: (archive.org scanned text of Genetti 2007, A Grammar of Dolakha Newar, MGL 40; title/CIP page confirms the work, ISBN 978-3-11-019303-9) and cross-checked against the project's local djvu text of Thurgood & LaPolla 2003 at line 31827). QUOTE: every clause of the reported quote is present verbatim at the stated locators, differing only by scanned line-break hyphens: p. 64 (txt lines 6324-6336, under page header '64 Chapter 2 Segmental phonetics and phonology / 5. Stress'): 'In Dolakha Newar, when words are pronounced in isolation, the first syllable is the most prominent, so can be said to be stressed. The primary cue for stress is pitch... Length does not seem to be relevant to stress'; p.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word prominence falls on the first syllable of the (phonological) word in citation forms, including on a verbal prefix when one is present (mwa-mwal patterns like a monomorphemic disyllable; p. 44: stress is on the 'phonetically initial syllable'); it is predictable and non-contrastive, cued mainly by an F0 peak on syllable 1 with steady fall thereafter, and the author explicitly hedges that the pattern might instead be an isolation-form intonation contour. Genetti 2003: 357 states it more flatly: 'Dolakhae has stress but no tone. Stress falls on the initial syllable of a root'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Genetti 2003: 357: 'with a secondary stress on third syllables in longer words.' Genetti 2007: 64 instead reports that in trisyllables pronounced in isolation prominence (F0 and intensity) decreases with each successive syllable; no secondary-stress rule is stated in the 2007 grammar.
new_statements.exceptions: None lexical. Clitics/particles and several bound morphemes are described as not independently stressed (e.g. pp. ~97-105, 250ff.); Nepali loans not singled out for stress. The only caveat is analytic: stress vs. isolation intonation undecided, 'very low functional load'.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly citation/isolation forms of the phonological word (root plus prefixes, suffixes and enclitics; first-syllable stress is listed as criterion (3) for phonological wordhood). In connected speech 'the word-level stress pattern is often obscured by the phrasal intonation contours' and 'lexical stress is thus subordinated to phrasal intonation' (pp. 66-67). No tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe Dolakha Newar (Dolakhae), the variety spoken in Dolakha village ~145 km east of Kathmandu; Glottolog 5.1 treats Dolakha Newar as the reference variety of the language-level languoid east2773 'Eastern Newari' (no separate dialect glottocode; ISO [new] is shared with Kathmandu Valley Newari newa1246). Statement should be catalogued as Dolakha Newar = east2773, not as Kathmandu Newar.
